teachingPoints.text: The goal of this video is a worked example of a menu-driven console program.
The program will build a simple menu of numbered options that the user picks from.
The options can be shown in a different order than the code defines, so menu entries are kept as data.
The set of options can be determined dynamically instead of being hardcoded.
An enum represents the available actions, giving each one a named constant instead of a bare number.
A second approach stores actions in a list and converts the user-selected index into the action stored at that position.
A third approach stores both the enum member identifying the action and the function that performs it, so each entry carries its own implementation.
Storing a function as a value lets a menu entry describe both what to do and how to do it.
The demo menu uses three options so the whole pattern fits in one short example.
The first menu option sums two numbers the user types in the console.
The second menu option greets the user after prompting for a name in the console.
The third menu option generates a random number.
The menu packages three smaller programs into one and only decides which of them runs.
The three actions share one program context and are never launched as separate processes, so all work happens at function level.
To dispatch on a menu choice the action must be representable as a program value, which the enum provides.
The enum declares three members: Addition for adding two numbers, Greeting for greeting the user, and RandomNumber for random number generation.
The menu loop has three parts: an enum naming the actions, reading the chosen option, and executing the action bound to that option.
The chosen action can be dispatched with if statements or a switch statement, as shown in an earlier video.
Dispatch is written as an ExecuteAction function that takes the action to run as a parameter.
Inside ExecuteAction the action value selects which function is called, for example Addition runs the sum function and Greeting runs the greeting function.
If the action value matches no known enum member the switch has no matching branch, so it must be treated as an error.
The menu therefore needs separate functions for the enum members Addition, Greeting and RandomNumber, each called from its own branch.
The using System.Diagnostics directive moves to the top of the file because the switch calls Debug.Fail.
The separate functions are implemented starting with Addition, which prompts for each number and tries to parse the input as an int.
If the input cannot be parsed as an int the loop starts over and asks again.
This retry-on-parse-failure loop pattern was covered in earlier videos, so the lesson does not dwell on it.
The parsed int must be declared outside the loop and the loop needs a break, so the value survives after the loop ends.
Because the same reading logic is needed for both A and B, it is extracted into a helper ReadIntIn that takes the variable name as a string.
The helper returns the parsed result and prints the supplied variable name instead of a hardcoded A.
Both A and B are read through the ReadIntIn helper instead of duplicated inline code.
The reading loop itself was explained in the dedicated input video, so it is only referenced here.
Addition then computes a plus b and prints the resulting sum.
The greet-user function is declared static void because it returns no value and only asks the user for a name.
Random number is the simplest remaining action because generating a number requires first obtaining an object that produces random values.
In C# the random generator is available as the static property Random.Shared, which you can call to get a random number.
The main function now handles reading the option number and interpreting it as an action.
The menu numbers are mapped to actions: 0 adds two numbers, 1 greets the user, and 2 prints a random number.
The option is read with ReadInt and then validated: if it is less than 0 or greater than 2 the input code runs again.
The option is read with ReadInt and validated by rerunning the input block plus printing an error whenever it is less than 0 or greater than 2.
After the read and validation the number in the variable holds the option, and a separate variable of the action type is declared at the top of the method.
The validated number only has to be interpreted as the action enum, which is safe because the check already proved the value lies between 0 and 2.
Repeating the read whenever the value falls outside 0 to 2 guarantees that after the check the value is always inside the valid range.
The number from 0 to 2 is cast directly to the action enum, using the same enum behavior shown earlier.
The validation loop is moved into its own static method that returns the action, keeping the main function readable.
What remains is an ExecuteAction step that reads the action and calls the function matching the action the user picked.
ExecuteAction calls the function that corresponds to whichever action the user entered.
A user cannot type a function itself as a console value, so the program must accept something else to select an action.
The user could either type the number that matches a function or type a string containing that function name.
This version deliberately requires the user to enter the number corresponding to the function, not its name.
Calling a function by a name string is impossible here because the call is resolved statically at compile time and becomes a direct call by address.
The selection logic is extended so the option can also be chosen by function name instead of only by its number.
Since a name string cannot be converted to int, the validation has to be rewritten: the function is copied out and the input string is checked before any conversion is attempted.
Before trying to convert the input to an int, the code first checks whether the string the user typed is one of the allowed option names.
Each allowed string (addition, greeting, random number) is compared with the input and the matching action is returned.
Generalizing this chain of string comparisons with reflection is possible but is intentionally not shown in this video.
C# lets you obtain the string bound to a name, so nameof(Addition) yields "Addition" as a string.
nameof works on functions too and the compiler substitutes the member name as a string, so renaming the function changes the string automatically.
Manually typing a different name instead of using nameof breaks compilation, while an editor rename updates the nameof string consistently.
Using a deliberately wrong placeholder name in the code turns the mismatch into a compile error, so the mistake is caught by the compiler and an editor rename updates every usage of that symbol.
The == comparison checks option names one after another, and the resulting rename is applied while the project compiles with dotnet build rather than when the program runs.
Renaming a menu entry this way is fully equivalent to typing the new name into the hardcoded string, so the option label can never drift out of sync with the code.

Running the program shows the renamed option is accepted when its number is entered, while a letter input is rejected and a valid number produces the expected result, confirming the rename propagated correctly.

Entering the new option name spelled with letters dispatches the greeting function, and entering the random-number option by number still prints a random value, so both input styles work after the rename.
Everything works, but the code now has a problem: the full list of options is written out a second time.
Each option is mentioned in two places, once in the source code and once in the printed string, so the duplicated lists can drift apart.
Adding a new function after the random number means also editing the printed string to insert a comma and the new number, and nothing connects that number to the function semantically.
No matter what is added to the program, the new option must be linked semantically to its action, and the fix is to introduce a dedicated Option class.
A new Option class is created so that each option carries a name, an action that runs when the user selects it, and later a description.
The Option class also carries a description field, so an option can describe itself to the user.
For every option in turn the code prints its index, its name and its description, so one loop can render the whole menu.
After printing, the input is compared against the option names and indexes and the matching action is selected by index.
To simplify this, a list holding all the actions as Option objects is created in one place instead of being scattered across the function.
The list is filled with options for addition, for greeting and for random number, each giving its name, its description and its action.
Because the options now live in one list they can be placed in any order, the index is no longer bound directly to a specific action, and the program becomes more flexible.
The options list is now passed into the function because the further choice of action is based on it.
The function accepts the list of options as a parameter, because the later action selection is derived from that list.
The fixed prompt string is replaced with an Enter an option message and the printing loop continues afterwards.
A loop walks the options and prints each one as an index or a name followed by its description.
A period rather than a semicolon is printed after each option, deliberately avoiding extra list formatting for now.
To match a name the code loops over all options and, when an option name equals the user input, that option becomes the result and its action is returned.
If the loop over all options completes without a name match, nothing was found and execution falls through to parsing the input as a number.
After parsing succeeds the index is validated, and since the minimum valid index is zero any value below zero is an error.

The option-selection code validates the entered index against the array bounds, treating a value below zero or greater than or equal to the array length as an error, so a bad menu choice cannot crash the program.
An index greater than or equal to the length of the options list is also rejected as an error, since no such option exists.
Instead of converting the numeric index into an action, the code now takes the action object directly out of the options array, which removes the index-to-action translation step.
Options may be defined in any order because the array is only read by index, so addition now sits at position one rather than zero after the change.

Re-running the program with a differently spelled number such as a random number in letters still resolves the option and returns early without running the remaining code, confirming parsing of the option happens before execution.

Because the option list can now be built elsewhere, it can be created outside the main function, for example in a static Options class exposing an AddOption function that receives the list and fills it item by item.

Option registration is moved into a dedicated AddOptions function that receives the list as a parameter and adds entries one by one, which makes the set of available actions configurable rather than hardcoded.
The main function now calls AddOptions to set up the available actions, so configuration is injected into the program from one place.
The main function neither chooses which options exist nor contains the code that picks a concrete option from the list, which separates menu content from program flow.
The main function still needs no code for executing the chosen action itself, since execution lives in the dedicated action-dispatch function.
The main function only needs access to three functions: one that initializes the list, one that reads the actions, and one that selects the action, which keeps its coupling minimal.
Because no action is executed directly in the main function, it never needs direct access to the individual action implementations, so they can stay internal to their own class.
Without touching the main function, removing one entry from the options list removed that entry from the menu, showing that the configuration function alone controls what the program offers.
Only the configuration function was changed and the main function stayed identical, which shows the code keeps working for any number of registered actions.
The actions are currently stored as plain numbers, and the only place these numbers are used is the action-selection function.
If each option stored the action itself instead of a number that is later turned into an action, the numbers and the manual linking inside the action-execution function would no longer be needed.
Storing the action directly raises the question of whether actions could be represented in some other way than as in-memory numbers at all.
A second reason to change the representation is that if an action could be denoted as a function outright, the system would be extended simply by adding new functions.
If an action were denoted as a function directly, adding a new capability to the system would mean only writing that function and listing it among the options.
With functions as actions, even a private function could be registered, because it is never invoked by name and the options list only stores a reference to it.
Today a function cannot be made private because making it a valid action requires adding it to the action list with a number and adding its execution to the action-execution function.

Since the function is called from outside its class it cannot be private, but passing a direct reference at option-creation time would let it be invoked by reference, making its visibility irrelevant.
A delegate-based command is invoked through a reference rather than by name, so whether the target method is private no longer blocks the call from anywhere.
Because the call goes through a reference, external code can inject its own actions without touching the centralized dispatch code that finds the target action.
To explain how functions store variables, the lesson steps down to a lower level and reviews what functions actually are before going deeper into how they work.
Compiling C# source code converts the source instructions into IL (Intermediate Language), a bytecode form used by compiled programs.
The compiler reads the source code and produces IL, which is why the IL is what ends up inside the compiled artifact.
When the program is compiled, a DLL containing the IL is produced, so the DLL is where the intermediate code lives.
When a program is compiled, a DLL (Dynamic Link Library) containing that IL is produced.
The DLL contains the IL (Intermediate Language) representation of the program's code.
IL stores the instructions as numeric identifiers, so the result is no longer source code but instructions at a lower level.
The SharpLab site lets you paste your C# code and inspect the IL that the compiler produces from it.
In the IL listing you can see structures such as the Program class, its Main function, and the calls to your own functions and console output.
The exact IL instructions need not be memorized; only the idea that source code becomes lower-level instructions matters.
The IL translation step also happens when you run the dotnet build command shown earlier.
Running the executable loads the IL code, which the runtime then compiles further for the actual machine.
The runtime turns the IL into machine code for your system and processor, which is the only kind of code the processor understands.
The precise syntax of the assembly listing in SharpLab does not need to be learned, because only the IL-to-machine-code pipeline matters here.
IL is loaded at program start and recompiled into instructions your processor can execute directly, so Main itself ends up as such machine instructions.
The assembly-looking lines in SharpLab are only a readable view; each displayed instruction actually has a numeric code associated with it.
The numbers shown for the assembly instructions are only illustrative; the real point is that each machine instruction has its own code.
Each CPU architecture defines both the instructions it supports and their numeric codes, which is why machine code is processor-specific.
At startup .NET converts the IL into machine code matching the CPU that is running, so the same IL can execute on any machine.
dotnet run lets you go from source code to a running program without thinking about the IL step explicitly.
dotnet run still passes through the IL stage before machine code is produced, even though the intermediate step is hidden from you.
Simplified: your code's instructions become numbers at program start and are then kept in memory for execution.
Before execution the instructions of your source code are turned into plain numbers and kept in memory, because that is the only form the machine can work with.
A processor can execute only instructions already loaded into the computer's memory, so source code has to be converted and loaded before it runs.
Your program code exists in process memory as machine code, that is as instructions specific to your processor, not in the form in which you wrote it.
Each function's instructions occupy some address in memory, so the instructions of one function and of another function are placed at separate addresses in converted form.
A function call written in source code is not resolved by name in machine code, where only a reference to the function remains.
The machine code never mentions the source-level function name such as SamOperations, it only carries a reference to that function.
Concretely the machine code asks to call the function at address 900 and then to continue executing from address 900, which is how execution enters another function at all.
Console.WriteLine also exists somewhere in memory as console code loaded from the standard library rather than as your own code.
Calls to that library function have no name reference in machine code either and are resolved by accessing the address where its instructions sit in memory.

The example walks through a local function inside another function to show why addresses matter: Main is loaded at one address and SamOperations at another, each as its own block of machine instructions.
Even though a local function is bound to the current invocation of its enclosing function, its code is loaded into memory only once, which the compiler transformation makes possible.
When a local function is created it effectively becomes a static function, and the original call that read local variables is replaced by generated code passing references to those locals.
After that transformation the local function becomes an ordinary but private method, since it is not visible outside its class.
The compiler additionally mangles the generated name so another function with its own local function of the same source name cannot clash with it.
So although the local function appears to be created afresh on each call of the enclosing function, its code exists in memory only a single time.
This works because for functions that use local variables the compiler replaces the call with a call that passes references to the captured local variables.
The usage of the local function is rewritten into a request for the function by its address in machine code.
The usage of the local function is therefore rewritten into a request for the function by its address in machine code.
Using the local function in the code becomes a request for it by address in machine code.
The key idea to carry forward is that the code of functions falls into memory and becomes reachable by address.
Because functions are addressed rather than named, we can refer to them indirectly through their address, which is exactly what polymorphism is built on.
Polymorphism itself is deliberately deferred, since what it means is explained a little later in the lesson.
The locally declared Action in the example file is deleted so the discussion can continue with the built-in type.
C# has a built-in type named Action that represents a function without parameters, and it had earlier been shadowed by the locally declared Action because local names take priority.
Once the local Action is removed, the name Action in the code refers to the public delegate void Action from the standard library.
Because the void part makes it parameterless and a delegate type merely stores a reference to a function, an Action value is a function reference that ties the address-based picture together.
The option type is declared as Action, i.e. a delegate that stores a reference to a function which returns nothing and takes no parameters.
Invoking an Action means jumping to the first address of the referenced function, continuing execution from there and returning to the caller when the function finishes.
All the menu actions are extracted out of the main function into the separate MenuOptions class so the menu logic no longer lives inline.
The action methods are made private because they are never called by name from outside the class, only through the stored reference to their address.
Where the option value previously came from nameof, it is now taken as a direct reference to the function itself.
Assigning a static method to the variable writes into it a delegate reference bound to that object and that function, so the variable holds an address instead of a number.
The code being discussed puts a reference to the object and the function that references that code into the delegate variable.
In modern C# a delegate object created from a static function reference exists only once for the whole lifetime of the program.
Whenever a static function is mentioned in the program as an object reference of function type, the compiler caches the delegate object, so only one such object ever exists.
Just like any other symbol, the option name can still be produced with nameof by passing the function name there.
Inside nameof there is no function taking a delegate parameter; it is a compile-time operator that expands at compilation rather than a function executed at run time.
Even a static function that does nothing could be added to the same list as one of the options.
The nameof operator works like a macro that is expanded at compile time into the name written at that place.
The chosen name is not bound to the function's own name, so any identifier may be used for the option.
The rest of the code stays unchanged; only the way the action is invoked changes from a name-based lookup to a reference.
After running the program the same options appear, and selecting the first one calls the referenced function by address with the given parameters.
The code inside Main is left as it was, so only the storage representation of the option changes.
The field now stores a reference to the action itself, the function, instead of a number that previously represented that action and was converted later.
Storing a reference buys flexibility: menu actions can be defined separately, even outside the main function, as long as there is a way to add them to the list.
The only public member of the options class used for configuration is the add function, so the class exposes just one entry point.
The add function is the only public configuration entry point of the class, and in principle this class could even be moved into a separate file.
The variable holding a name or address decides what runs: different contents of that variable cause different actions to execute.
At the call site it is not known which function will run, because that depends on what was added to the list and which option the user chooses.
Calling one action while the concrete function is only decided at run time is called polymorphism.
Polymorphism means invoking an action not directly but through the address saved in a variable, which lets one call site run different functions.
